title: The Sunday Essay: In Defence of DISC
author: Richard Claydon
summary: Richard Claydon defends the thinking behind DISC while conceding that its modern corporate form is often ridiculous. He argues that zealots and cynics are reacting to the same flattened instrument, and that William Moulton Marston was not sorting fixed personality types but describing recurring responses to environments that feel antagonistic or allied, met actively or passively. Reread that way, the four letters become postures, namely Dominance, Compliance, Inducement and Submission, rather than traits belonging to the person. Using a composite leader called Maya and Kurt Lewin's B=f(P,E), he shows how workplace profiling drops the environment out of the picture and treats behaviour as inner essence. His proposal is to repurpose DISC as a field diagnostic that asks what postures an organisation keeps producing and what that reveals about its conditions of trust, threat and authority.
points: Zealots overbelieve and cynics overdismiss, and both are stuck at the level of the vulgarised instrument rather than the original idea.
Reading DISC as response to conditions makes it a map of postures people adopt under antagonistic or allied fields, so the same leader can show all four in one week.
Each posture has a healthy and a hardened form, for example situational firmness decaying into habitual overcontrol or receptivity into over-deference.
The deeper critique is that psychometric thinking looks inside the person and drops the environment, contrary to Lewin's point that behaviour is a function of person and environment.
Leaders can use the model diagnostically by asking which postures their organisation normalises and what conditions are producing them, instead of telling people to adapt to each other's styles.
quotes: DISC in its modern workplace form is indeed often ridiculous. But that does not mean William Moulton Marston was simply a crank making things up before psychology learned how to measure properly. It means, rather, that a richer model of behaviour may have been reduced into a weaker instrument: something dynamic made static, something situational made typological, something relational made personal.

Marston is worth defending not because the psychometric built on his work is stronger than its critics think, but because his underlying intuition is better. He was not really trying to sort stable personality types. He was trying to describe recurring patterns of response in relation to different kinds of environment.

Used badly, DISC flattens behaviour into type. Used more intelligently, it can become a rough way of reading environments: where force is normalised, where caution is trained, where persuasion substitutes for structure, and where trust still makes receptivity possible.
A type implies essence. A posture implies organisation in relation to circumstance. A type belongs to the person. A posture belongs to the encounter between person and field.

The same person may show Dominance in a project meeting, Compliance in front of an unpredictable executive, Inducement with peers, and Submission when working with a trusted mentor or expert. That is not inconsistency. It is situational organisation.

The real mistake modern psychometrics often makes is therefore not bad measurement, but premature closure. It asks, “What kind of person is this?” and stops too soon. It describes the individual more and more carefully while asking too little about the field in which that individual is acting.

That is why so much workplace diagnosis feels thin even when the instruments sound sophisticated. Better measurement of the person can coexist with poorer interpretation of the situation. The result is often a psychology that is technically sharper but ecologically weaker.
